result: The study analyzed a comprehensive global dataset of 1,303 S. Dublin genomes spanning four decades, including 53 Australian isolates and 1,250 from other continents. The dataset revealed ST10 as the dominant lineage (99.4%) with ST74 and ST1545 detected only in Australia.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the dataset's comprehensiveness and methodological rigor. Reviewer 3 notes this is 'the most comprehensive analysis of Salmonella Dublin to date,' while Reviewer 2 confirms 'methodology included...were sound and written in sufficient detail.' The only acknowledged limitation is geographic bias toward high-income settings, which reviewers accept as unavoidable.

result: Antimicrobial resistance analysis revealed strong geographical associations, with highly resistant MDR isolates (51.5% of genomes) confined predominantly to North America and linked to IncC plasmids encoding AMR and heavy metal resistance, while Australian isolates were largely susceptible.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings as part of the study's core contributions. Reviewer 2 notes the study 'unfolded the evolutionary history...highlighting clonal expansions linked to each distinct geography' and that 'North American ST10 was associated with more antimicrobial resistance.' Reviewer 1 describes the manuscript as uncovering 'distinct genotypic adaptations, antimicrobial resistance patterns' that are 'rigorous and compelling.'

result: Phylogenetic and phylodynamic analyses identified two distinct Australian lineages (ST10 and ST74), with ST10 remaining globally dominant. A small number of Australian ST10 isolates harbored a novel hybrid plasmid. The MRCA for the global population was estimated at 1901, with geographical clades emerging between 1950-2000.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support the phylogenetic findings. Reviewer 2 states the 'detailed genomic epidemiology of ST10 unfolded the evolutionary history of this common genotype' and notes the authors 'performed long read sequencing...and uncovered a novel recombinant virulence plasmid.' Reviewer 1 describes these as 'distinct genotypic adaptations' that are 'rigorous.' No concerns about the phylodynamic dating or clade structure were raised.

result: ST74 exhibited unique genomic features including a larger pangenome (1,143 ST74-specific genes vs. 473 ST10-specific genes), absence of SPI-19 encoding T6SS, and >900 uncharacterized genes. A minimum of 2,402 SNPs separated ST10 and ST74 lineages.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the comparative genomic analysis. Reviewer 2 notes 'comparative genomic analyses between the two genotypes showed certain genetic content unique to each genotype' and that the study provides 'novel understanding on the evolution and adaptation of two S. Dublin genotypes.' While Reviewer 2 mentions 'no further analyses were conducted to investigate which genetic factors likely associated with the observed differences,' this is stated as an observation rather than a critique undermining the findings.

result: ST74 displayed enhanced intracellular replication in human macrophages (up to 8-fold over 24 hours) compared to ST10 (less than 2-fold), while inducing significantly less pro-inflammatory responses and cytotoxicity at early timepoints (3 and 9 hpi), suggesting alternative virulence strategies.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support the virulence phenotyping results. Reviewer 2 states the authors 'performed cell invasion and cytotoxicity assays on the two S. Dublin genotypes, showing differential responses between the two STs' and that 'ST74 replicates better intracellularly in macrophage compared to ST10.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the phenotyping of isolates of ST10 and ST74...offer insights into the variability that can be seen in S. Dublin' and calls this a 'valuable contribution.'

result: In epithelial HT-29 cells, ST10 isolates showed more efficient replication (up to 10-fold in 6/11 isolates) compared to ST74 (minimal replication up to 2-fold), with minimal cytotoxicity observed across both lineages. By 24 hpi in macrophages, cytotoxicity was comparable between lineages.
evaluation: These findings are part of the virulence assessment that reviewers affirm. Reviewer 2 notes 'both STs induced comparable cytotoxicity levels' at later timepoints, consistent with these claims. The cell-type specific differences are encompassed in the reviewers' general approval of the phenotypic characterization showing 'differential responses between the two STs.'

result: The Vi antigen (viaB locus) was absent in 1,302/1,303 (99.9%) S. Dublin genomes including all ST10 and ST74 isolates, with implications for serotyping, vaccine development, and diagnostic strategies. Only one historical French isolate (SLV ST73) possessed the viaB operon.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the comprehensive genomic characterization. Reviewer 1 describes the study as uncovering findings with implications for 'epidemiological success,' which would include diagnostic and vaccine considerations. No reviewer questions the Vi antigen absence or its stated implications.

result: Heavy metal resistance determinants were ubiquitous (golS/golT in 99.9% of isolates) or highly prevalent (mer operon in 90.1% of IncC plasmid-carrying isolates). IncX1 (97.4%) and IncFII(S) (93.1%) plasmid replicons were found at high frequency, with one Australian isolate harboring a novel hybrid plasmid lacking the spv operon.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the plasmid analysis findings. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes the authors 'uncovered a novel recombinant virulence plasmid in ST10 (IncX1/IncFII/IncN)' and that the study provides 'comprehensive and novel understanding.' The heavy metal resistance patterns are part of the 'antimicrobial resistance patterns' that Reviewer 1 describes as rigorously characterized.

result: Virulence factor screening showed most isolates had high predicted invasiveness scores (>0.5 in 99.16%), with universal or near-universal presence of pagN (100%) and pgtE (99.9%). ST313-associated features (ST313-gi, Gifsy-2 prophage, ggt) were present in ST10 but absent in ST74. SPI-6 showed variable coverage in 32.4% of genomes.
evaluation: These genomic characterization findings are part of the comprehensive analysis that reviewers affirm. Reviewer 2 confirms 'data analysis were performed with rigour' and 'source data were fully presented and accessible.' The virulence factor distribution contributes to understanding the 'virulence strategies' that Reviewer 1 describes as rigorously characterized.

result: Background claims establish S. Dublin as a host-adapted, bovine-associated invasive NTS serovar causing bloodstream infections in humans, with increasing AMR prevalence. It is transmitted through contaminated dairy/meat and represents a One Health pathogen causing significant global morbidity.
evaluation: These are well-established background claims supported by citations that reviewers do not question. Reviewer 3 notes the study 'offers insights into the global spread of this pathogen' and Reviewer 1 describes it as examining an important invasive pathogen, implicitly accepting the background characterization.

result: Literature-based claims describe previously reported MDR S. Dublin lineages in North America (ST10 with IncC plasmids), S. Dublin's relationship to S. Enteritidis/Gallinarum, the existence of ST74 as a distinct lineage, and the presence of two T6SS-encoding SPIs (SPI-6 and SPI-19) with roles in interbacterial competition.
evaluation: These are established literature claims that provide context for the study's novel findings. Reviewers do not question these background assertions. Reviewer 2 notes the 'rewritten Discussion is more relevant and brings in comparison with other invasive Salmonella serotypes,' indicating acceptance of the contextual framework.

result: All isolates including ST74 were serotyped in silico as S. Dublin, though ST74 and one ST10 isolate showed distinct fliC codon profiles. The phylogeographic patterns are consistent with previous studies and likely reflect livestock movement patterns, including historical cattle imports from USA to Australia in the 1930s.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these interpretive and contextual findings. Reviewer 2 confirms the authors 'addressed all the points raised' in revision, and Reviewer 3 notes the study 'offers insights into the global spread of this pathogen and region-specific traits.' The historical livestock movement interpretation is not questioned.

result: Clinical source analysis showed ST74 human isolates (n=7) were from fecal samples (gastroenteritis cases), while 18/40 ST10 isolates were from invasive disease sites (blood or abscess), suggesting different clinical presentations between lineages.
evaluation: This clinical correlation is part of the phenotypic characterization that reviewers affirm. Reviewer 3 specifically notes the study 'reminds the field that it is important to look beyond lab-adapted strains to truly understand these pathogens,' implicitly supporting the clinical diversity findings. No reviewer questions the clinical source data.

result: The authors speculate that loss of the spv operon in the novel hybrid plasmid may be associated with a less invasive phenotype, based on literature citation.
evaluation: This is a speculative interpretation clearly marked as such in the manuscript. Reviewers do not challenge this speculation, and it is presented appropriately as a hypothesis rather than a definitive conclusion. The speculation is based on cited literature and is part of the plasmid characterization that reviewers affirm.
